figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Interactive world generation with Hy-Nomas. Free-form text instructions and continuous camera control can be interleaved across successive interaction turns. At each turn, a vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts the user request and observed world history into a structured text prompt and a duration for the next video segment. Conditioned on these inputs and cached context, Hy-Nomas autoregressively generates the next segment, allowing the world to unfold through continued interaction.
figures.headline: Interleaved text and camera instructions drive successive generated segments, each prompted by a Prompt Enhancer from history.
citing_sentences: Hy-Nomas can generate visual worlds with different styles and viewpoints, supporting minute-scale rollouts with successive instructions for subject actions, object interactions, scene changes and camera motion, as shown in Figure 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Data pipeline. Raw videos are split, transcoded, and filtered by basic video properties and visual quality. Hierarchical clustering supports within-cluster deduplication, and a VLM assigns labels to each video from a predefined taxonomy. Video tagging adds captions and, for selected clips, camera-trajectory annotations. Across each training stage, adaptive sampling adjusts the training distribution in response to weaknesses identified from evaluations of earlier stages.
figures.headline: The data pipeline filters raw videos, deduplicates clusters, labels a taxonomy, and adds captions and trajectories.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Structured video captioning. The VLM annotates segments sequentially, maintains subject identities, interleaves scene and camera descriptions chronologically, and records subject actions separately with timestamps. A final text-only turn reviews, translates, and validates the annotations to produce aligned English and Chinese captions. During training, camera-motion sentences and their tags are removed when camera trajectories are available and retained otherwise.
figures.headline: Multi-turn annotation produces aligned English and Chinese captions with chronological descriptions and timestamped actions.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 and 4 illustrates the caption design and multi-turn annotation procedure.
During preprocessing, each video segment is annotated with a structured JSON caption, as illustrated in Figure 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Structured caption format. Video-level fields define perspective, style, and shared subject profiles. Segment descriptions interleave scene information and camera-tagged motion chronologically, excluding main-subject references. The first segment provides a full description; later segments describe changes. Subject actions and their visible outcomes are recorded separately in action-tagged entries using subject tokens. Action intervals are non-overlapping and remain within segment boundaries.
figures.headline: The structured caption format stores subject profiles, chronological segment descriptions, and non-overlapping timestamped actions.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 and 4 illustrates the caption design and multi-turn annotation procedure.
It produces the final English caption and a structurally aligned Chinese translation, both following the format in Figure 4.

PE returns video-level metadata and the first segment caption, including visual_description_long to establish the scene and contained_actions to specify subject actions, according to the caption format defined in Figure 4.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Overview of the model architecture. A structured multi-segment prompt, a video clip, and a camera trajectory are encoded into text, video, and camera tokens, respectively. Text and video tokens are processed by $N=54$ dual-stream MMDiT blocks. Within each block, segment-wise causal attention with 3D RoPE allows tokens to attend to the current and preceding segments, while diffusion timestep embeddings modulate both streams. The two streams pass through separate MLPs, and camera cross-attention further conditions the video stream on camera tokens. During autoregressive generation, keys and values associated with both text and video tokens are stored in the KV cache as context for subsequent segments. The 3D VAE decoder maps denoised video latents to RGB frames. Purple, blue, and green denote the text, video, and camera streams, respectively.
figures.headline: Text, video and camera tokens pass through dual-stream blocks, with earlier segments cached for later generation.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 illustrates the architecture, and Table 1 summarizes its primary configuration.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Comparison of segment-wise and action-aware causal attention. (a) Tokens attend to all video and text tokens in the current and preceding segments. (b) Action-aware masking further restricts access to action-specific text tokens. Colors indicate query-to-key modality pairs; gray cells are masked. head denotes the environment description for the current segment, and $a_{0},\ldots,a_{n}$ denote actions within that segment.
figures.headline: Action-aware masking restricts action text to its own segment, whereas segment-wise masking exposes all earlier tokens.
citing_sentences: We illustrate this design in Figure 6(a).

To address these issues, we introduce action-aware causal attention, which extends segment-wise causal attention with a finer-grained masking scheme to distinguish actions within and across segments, as illustrated in Figure 6(b).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Segment Forcing with streaming backward. Each current segment receives a flow-matching loss; a one-step low-noise estimation supplies cached context for later segments. Streaming backward retains only one segment’s computation graph at a time, accumulating gradients for a single optimizer step after the full sequence. The cache update of the final segment is skipped.
figures.headline: Segment forcing trains on the model's own low-noise context, holding one segment's computation graph in memory at a time.
citing_sentences: The complete pipeline is illustrated in Figure 7.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Downstream LoRA adaptation workflow. Train LoRA adapters on the base autoregressive model (before distillation), then merge the learned weights into the distilled model for efficient deployment, without full-model fine-tuning or repeating distillation.
figures.headline: LoRA adapters trained before distillation are merged into the distilled model, avoiding full fine-tuning or repeated distillation.
citing_sentences: The workflow is illustrated in Figure 8.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Prompt Enhancer (PE) workflow. PE generates an initial dense caption in the first turn. In subsequent turns, users can choose text prompts or camera control, and PE combines the selected input with the full interaction history to generate a dense caption that AR-DiT uses to produce the next video segment. Each turn’s dialogue and generated video are appended to the history.
figures.headline: Prompt Enhancer generates a caption each turn from the user input and full history, in either text or camera mode.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Overview of Hy-Nomas-Bench. Top: Model outputs for an example case from Bench-3 (interleaved text–camera control). Bottom: (a) World settings span diverse scenes, visual styles, subjects, and viewpoints. (b) 280 cases cover multi-turn text interaction, camera navigation, interleaved control, and spatial memory. (c) Unified control maps instructions to text, binary key states $[T,8]$ (W/A/S/D and four arrow keys), or per-frame $4\times 4$ camera-to-world matrices $[T,4,4]$, where $T$ is the frame count. Generation continues across turns without world resets. (d) Three annotators evaluate prompt following, physical plausibility, camera control, and memory consistency through pairwise comparisons. Results are summarized by win/tie/loss rates and net win rate (win minus loss, in percentage points).
figures.headline: Hy-Nomas-Bench covers text, camera, interleaved and memory cases, with unified control inputs and pairwise human ratings.
citing_sentences: The overview of Hy-Nomas-Bench is shown in Figure 10.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Illustration of the design of Bench-4: Spatial memory. Each uses a static anchor object and four outbound–return pairs. Bench-4 evaluates object permanence under different camera movements, and appearance/layout consistency. Left: Different trajectory types. Center: Scene, camera frustum, and trajectory. Right: Inference results by Hy-Nomas.
figures.headline: Bench-4 uses a static anchor object and outbound-return camera trajectories to test whether it reappears consistently.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 illustrates the anchor-based camera trajectory designs.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison of multi-turn text interaction. In the first example, Hy-Nomas clearly shows the apple being grasped, lifted, and brought to the plate. LingBot-World v2 changes the apple’s color and gripper structure, while HappyOyster-Directing shows discontinuous views without a clear grasp-and-lift progression. In the second example, Hy-Nomas visualizes the requested spatula, cutting on the board, and strawberries in the glass bowl. LingBot-World v2 only shows cutting strawberries and a knife without spatula, while HappyOyster-Directing does not move strawberries into the bowl.
figures.headline: In the apple example, Hy-Nomas shows a clear grasp-and-lift sequence, while LingBot-World v2 changes the apple's color.
citing_sentences: Figures 12 provides qualitative examples for multi-turn text interaction.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Pairwise human evaluation of multi-turn text control. We compare Hy-Nomas with HappyOyster-Directing and LingBot-World v2 on prompt following and physical plausibility. Within each evaluation dimension, the two 100% stacked bars show wins (green), ties (gray), and losses (pink) from the perspective of Hy-Nomas.
figures.headline: Hy-Nomas wins 65.0% against HappyOyster-Directing and 75.0% against LingBot-World v2 on prompt following.
citing_sentences: Figure 13 summarizes the results.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison of camera control in an indoor scene. Rows show Hy-Nomas (Ours), LingBot-World v2, HappyOyster-Wandering, and Genie 3. The comparison illustrates how each model responds to navigation commands while maintaining a third-person view of the character and the surrounding room. The middle frame of LingBot-World v2 shows a duplicated character, illustrating a scene-consistency failure during navigation. Visible keyboard indicators denote active controls in the source recordings.
figures.headline: LingBot-World v2 duplicates the character in a middle frame of an indoor navigation example, a scene-consistency failure.
citing_sentences: Figure 14 complements these results with an indoor navigation example.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Pairwise human evaluation of camera control. We compare Hy-Nomas with Genie 3, HappyOyster-Wandering, and LingBot-World v2 on 100 shared trajectories. We measure how accurately the model responds to navigation commands.
figures.headline: Hy-Nomas achieves higher win than loss rates against all three models on 100 shared camera-control trajectories.
citing_sentences: Figure 15 presents the results on camera control across all four models.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Pairwise human evaluation of interleaved text and camera control. We compare Hy-Nomas with the adapted LingBot-World v2 baseline on 60 scenarios with alternating text and camera inputs. We consider prompt following, physical plausibility, and camera control during the evaluation.
figures.headline: Against adapted LingBot-World v2 on interleaved cases, Hy-Nomas wins 75.0% on prompt following and 73.3% on plausibility.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 16, Hy-Nomas achieves win rate of 75.0% and 73.3% in prompt following and physical plausibility, respectively.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Pairwise human evaluation of spatial memory. We compare Hy-Nomas with Genie 3, HappyOyster, and LingBot-World v2 on 60 shared scenarios involving reversible or revisiting camera trajectories. We measure how well the model remembers the anchor object and its surrounding environments.
figures.headline: Hy-Nomas wins 13.3% and loses 30.0% against Genie 3 on spatial memory, but wins 58.3% against LingBot-World v2.
citing_sentences: Figure 17 presents the results of the spatial memory evaluation.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison of spatial memory under viewpoint revisitation. Rows show Hy-Nomas (Ours), LingBot-World v2, HappyOyster-Wandering, and Genie 3; columns show successive frames from a camera-only rollout. Hy-Nomas and Genie 3 retain the closed toolbox in revisited views, whereas LingBot-World v2 changes it to an open toolbox. This case illustrates object-state consistency; aggregate results in Figure 17 provide the broader comparison.
figures.headline: A red toolbox stays closed in Hy-Nomas and Genie 3 revisited views, but opens in LingBot-World v2.
citing_sentences: Figure 18 illustrates a spatial memory example in a scene with a red toolbox on a wooden workbench.

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: Qualitative results of LoRA-SFT. We compare the distilled model with domain-specific LoRA-SFT variants. The upper examples show improved cinematic aesthetics after cinematic LoRA-SFT, while the lower examples show more physically plausible robotic manipulation, with cup deformation more faithfully reflecting the gripper’s applied pressure. LoRA-SFT denotes the distilled model with the trained LoRA weights merged into it.
figures.headline: The cinematic LoRA model shows stronger cinematic styling, and the robotics LoRA shows cup deformation matching grip pressure.
citing_sentences: Compared with the distilled model, the cinematic LoRA-adapted model produces a more visually appealing cinematic style, as illustrated in Figure 19.

Compared to the distilled model as a baseline, illustrated in Figure 19, the merged robotics-specific distilled checkpoint can perform out-of-distribution dual-arm tasks, while the baseline confuses the generation of dual-arm and human hands due to the heavy training set distribution of human egocentric data.

figures.label: Figure 20
figures.caption: Pairwise human evaluation of cinematic LoRA-SFT against the distilled model. We evaluate prompt following and physical plausibility on Bench-1, and camera control on Bench-2. The three 100% stacked bars show wins (green), ties (gray), and losses (pink) from the perspective of LoRA-SFT relative to the base model. LoRA-SFT denotes the distilled model with the trained LoRA weights merged into it.
figures.headline: LoRA-SFT wins 35% on prompt following and 46% on physical plausibility, but camera control drops, with 37% losses.
citing_sentences: Quantitative results are reported in Figure 20.

figures.label: Figure 21
figures.caption: Rank-gap-weighted human evaluation of Hy-Nomas-PE (ours). Bench-1 and bench-3 are reported separately; each pair compares Hy-Nomas-PE with Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-K3. Bench-1 evaluates prompt following and physical plausibility; bench-3 also evaluates camera control. Category labels are shared within each benchmark. Each 100% stacked bar shows win (green), tie (gray), and loss (pink) votes from the perspective of Hy-Nomas-PE.
figures.headline: Hy-Nomas-PE improves over Qwen3.8-27B and narrows the gap with Kimi-K3 in rank-gap-weighted human evaluation.
citing_sentences: Figure 21 presents the evaluation results on Bench-1 and Bench-3.

abstract: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.

sections.body: Hy-Nomas is an 8B-parameter video world model that accepts free-form text instructions and continuous camera control over several interaction turns. The introduction lists the difficulties: adapting a bidirectional diffusion transformer to causal generation, preventing errors from compounding across generated segments, keeping persistent scene information while action instructions apply only within their time window, and connecting text commands with camera motion. The authors name four contributions: the model, aligned captions with action-aware attention, a multi-stage training recipe with bounded-cache inference and LoRA adaptation, and an evaluation with released benchmarks. The text states that temporally causal information flow alone does not establish physical causality.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Hy-Nomas is an 8B interactive world model that follows free-form text and camera commands across multiple turns.

sections.body: The corpus mixes real and virtual videos. Raw videos are split into 5-minute segments, cut at detected shot boundaries, transcoded, and filtered by duration, aspect ratio, resolution, motion, clarity and aesthetic scores. Visual embeddings are hierarchically clustered, and SemDeDup removes redundant clips within each cluster. A fine-tuned vision-language model assigns taxonomy labels used for data selection. ViPE estimates camera trajectories for a subset of videos, and a video-based inverse dynamics model predicts discrete camera motion to flag inconsistent labels. Trajectory filters check optical flow, CoTracker3 displacement, AnyCalib focal-length changes and optimization failures. Captions are structured JSON produced through multi-turn annotation. Adaptive sampling reweights subsets between training stages to address weaknesses found earlier.
sections.heading: Data
sections.headline: Training videos are filtered, deduplicated, and annotated with camera trajectories and structured captions.

sections.body: Hy-Nomas builds on HunyuanVideo 1.5 and uses a DCAE-V video autoencoder with 32× spatial and 4× temporal compression, a frozen Qwen2.5-VL-7B text encoder, and 54 dual-stream MMDiT blocks. Attention is bidirectional within a segment and causal across segments. Action-aware causal attention splits each segment's text into a descriptive head and action tails. Heads stay accessible to later segments, while each action tail is restricted to its originating segment and time window. The text says this reduces action-order errors and cross-segment action repetition. Camera poses are converted to relative frame-to-frame transforms, grouped into 64-dimensional vectors, and injected through cross-attention in every block. During training, camera conditioning is randomly disabled per segment, and camera descriptions are removed from captions for camera-conditioned segments.
sections.heading: Model Architecture
sections.headline: Action-aware causal attention limits each action to its own time window, and camera tokens condition each segment.

sections.body: Training combines eight-GPU Ulysses sequence parallelism, data parallelism across replicas, and FSDP2 sharding within each group. Sequences reach up to 360K tokens, with each rank holding approximately 45K tokens at maximum sequence length. FLOPs-balanced packing estimates per-sample cost from token count and unmasked query-key pairs, then assigns packs to replicas with a greedy longest-processing-time-first rule. A flex-flash attention kernel from MagiAttention handles segment and action masks without materializing dense masks. Muon optimizes attention and feed-forward weight matrices, and AdamW handles the remaining parameters. The text reports that retaining attention outputs during segment forcing would add approximately 1.6 GB per rank without a meaningful speed gain, so that stage uses ordinary recomputation. Checkpoints are saved asynchronously with dataloader states for deterministic resumption.
sections.heading: Training Infrastructure
sections.headline: Sequence parallelism, compute-balanced packing and masked attention kernels support training on sequences up to 360K tokens.

sections.body: The curriculum has three tracks: causality, interaction and context length. Stage 1 adapts the VAE to a more compact latent space, with 20K steps updating input and output layers followed by 60K full-model steps. Stage 2 runs segment-causal continual pre-training, then action-aware training on temporally localized action captions that expands context from 180K to 360K tokens, then camera-conditioned training with trajectory and non-trajectory videos mixed at a 1:1 ratio. Stage 3 anneals on high-quality videos captioned by Kimi K3, raising maximum text length from 768 to 1,280 tokens. Stage 4 applies segment forcing to a subset of that data. Stage 5 distills the model from 100 to 4 NFEs per segment, starting from a causal Phased Consistency Model initialization and refining under hybrid forcing.
sections.heading: Model Training
sections.headline: Training proceeds through causal, interaction and context curricula, then distillation from 100 to 4 steps per segment.

sections.body: The Prompt Enhancer (PE) receives a system prompt, the current user input, the dialogue history and previously generated segments, and returns a structured caption for the next segment. The first turn produces video metadata and a first-segment caption. Later text turns produce description changes and next-segment actions. Camera-control turns produce only description changes, with the user trajectory passed separately to the generator. PE is a lightweight model trained with supervised fine-tuning from Qwen3.8-27B on multi-turn conversations. For single-GPU inference, the system uses INT8 weights and cached keys and values, sliding-window attention, CPU offloading, and sparse attention that keeps 25% of candidate video blocks after the first two denoising steps. A 100-second video across seven segments at 1280×704 and 24 FPS requires 20.53 GiB of peak GPU memory. The text notes that these optimizations may introduce differences that become more noticeable across segments.
sections.heading: Model Inference
sections.headline: A vision-language Prompt Enhancer turns user requests into segment captions, and inference is optimized for a single device.

sections.body: Hy-Nomas-Bench contains 280 cases in four benchmarks: multi-turn text (60 scenarios with 2–6 turns), camera navigation (100 cases), interleaved text and camera (60 cases with 2–7 segments), and spatial memory (60 scenarios). Groups of three annotators give pairwise win, tie and loss judgments on prompt following, physical plausibility, camera control and memory consistency. On Bench-1, Hy-Nomas wins 65.0% against HappyOyster-Directing and 75.0% against LingBot-World v2 on prompt following, and wins 45.0% and 68.3% on physical plausibility. On spatial memory against Genie 3, Hy-Nomas wins 13.3%, ties 56.7% and loses 30.0%. The text states that Genie 3 maintains stronger long-term spatial consistency than Hy-Nomas.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Human raters prefer Hy-Nomas over three interactive world models on most tasks, but Genie 3 leads on spatial memory.

sections.body: The related work groups world models into representation-based approaches such as V-JEPA, geometry-based systems such as World Labs, reconstruction models such as VGGT, and video-based approaches. Video-based world models include Genie, Genie 2 and Genie 3, LingBot-World v2, and HappyOyster, which the authors evaluate. The section also covers video diffusion, including Diffusion Transformers and Self Forcing, which trains on model-generated histories. The authors position Hy-Nomas in the video-based line, combining temporally structured supervision, persistent causal context and a VLM-based director in one 8B model. The section states that whether scaling alone yields physical dynamics remains an open research question.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Hy-Nomas is placed among video-based world models that add text and camera control to diffusion video generators.

sections.body: For gaming, the paper flags response latency and notes that distillation and quantization reduce cost, but must be checked against visual quality and consistency over long rollouts. For robotics, predicted outcomes must match executable robot actions, which requires training on videos paired with robot actions. The authors say Open X-Embodiment coverage remains limited and present LoRA robotics fine-tuning as an initial step. For long-horizon memory, the text proposes offloading older context and retrieving relevant segments, and notes that retrieval cannot update states that change outside the field of view, such as a clock. The authors hypothesize that detailed captions contribute to the 8B model's text-driven control, a hypothesis they state rather than test.
sections.heading: Discussion and Future Directions
sections.headline: Discussion names open challenges: response latency, action-grounded robotics, retrieval-based memory, and detailed caption quality.

sections.body: This section lists the people who contributed to Hy-Nomas. It has four groups: core contributors, contributors, acknowledgments, and leadership acknowledgments. Within each group, names are listed in alphabetical order by last name. The section contains no methods, results or claims beyond the attribution of work.
